summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Black populations and the meaning of 'blackness' across regions. It covers the historical Arab and Atlantic slave trades and their demographic legacies, including Afro-descendant communities in the Arab world, South Asia, Spain, the Americas, the UK, Montenegro, and Southeast Asia. It also discusses political representation, the shifting use of the term 'black' (including Toni Morrison's and Christopher Hitchens's remarks about Bill Clinton), and classification debates.
one_line: Overview of Black populations worldwide, their histories of enslavement and migration, and how 'blackness' is defined and classified across regions.
key_facts: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur ruled Morocco from 1578 to 1608 and was not technically considered a mixed-race child of a slave; his mother was Fulani and a concubine of his father.

Historians estimate 10 to 18 million sub-Saharan Black Africans were enslaved by Arab slave traders between the advent of Islam in 650CE and the mid-20th century abolition of slavery in the Arabian Peninsula.
Arab slave traders shipped more female slaves than males because there was demand for them as concubines in harems, and male slaves were castrated to serve as harem guards.
Approximately 12 million Africans were shipped to the Americas during the Atlantic slave trade from 1492 to 1888, with Brazil importing 5.5 million African slaves.

The Siddi of India and Pakistan are descended from Bantu peoples from Southeast Africa; the term 'Siddi' derives from 'Sayyid', the title of captains of Arab vessels that brought settlers to the area.
Afro-Spaniards are Spanish nationals of West/Central African descent, and there were an estimated 683,000 Afro-Spaniards in Spain.
In early 1991, non-Arab Zaghawa people of Sudan attested that they were victims of an intensifying Arab apartheid campaign.
Toni Morrison described Bill Clinton as the first black President of the United States, citing 'almost every trope of blackness'.
At the 2001 census there were over a million black people in the United Kingdom: 1% described themselves as 'Black Caribbean', 0.8% as 'Black African', and 0.2% as 'Black other'.
The Empire Windrush is named as the first symbolic movement of Caribbean workers encouraged to immigrate to Britain after World War II.
The town of Ulcinj in Montenegro had a black community; until 1878, 100 black people lived there as a consequence of the Ottoman slave trade and privateer activity.
The Ottoman Army deployed an estimated 30,000 Black African troops and cavalrymen to its expedition in Hungary during the Austro-Turkish War of 1716–18.
In 1619, John Rolfe used the term 'negars' to describe slaves captured from West Africa and shipped to the Virginia colony.
The Negritos are believed to be the first inhabitants of Southeast Asia, and the term Negrito means 'little black people' in Spanish.
Iraq has a reported 1.2 million black people, and African-Iraquis have sought minority status that would reserve some seats in Parliament.
According to Alamin M. Mazrui et al., most people of visible African descent in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries still classify and identify as Arab, not black.
